claims.claim: The universe is everything that exists: the totality of time and space and all of the matter and energy in them - the entire cosmos.
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old; NASA dates its beginning to a rapid expansion some 13.8 billion years ago.
The observable universe contains billions of galaxies, and survey missions map galaxies found up to 10 billion light-years from Earth.

Galaxies are arranged in large-scale structures: groups and clusters of galaxies bound together by gravity, superclusters gathering clusters and groups, and twisting, threadlike filaments called the cosmic web, with huge voids between the structures.

Distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the more distant a galaxy is, the faster it recedes - a direct proportionality known as Hubble's law (v = H x d), established by Edwin Hubble in 1929 and with Milton Humason in 1931; the universe is expanding.

Dark matter is inferred from its gravitational effects: the rotation curves of spiral galaxies, the motions of galaxies within clusters, and gravitational lensing all reveal more mass than visible matter can account for; dark matter does not absorb, reflect, or emit light.

Dark energy is the name given to the unknown driver of the accelerating expansion of the universe, recognized from supernova observations in the late 1990s; it is part of the current model, and its nature is not yet known.
In the current model of the universe, ordinary matter makes up about 5% of the contents, dark matter about 27%, and dark energy about 68%.
Astronomers study the universe by collecting light from distant objects with telescopes, which work across the electromagnetic spectrum.

sourceRecords.title: What is Dark Energy? Inside Our Accelerating, Expanding Universe
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (canonical URL https://science.nasa.gov/dark-energy/; the /universe/dark-energy/ path returns 404). Supports: the universe began with a rapid expansion some 13.8 billion years ago; about nine billion years after the beginning the expansion started speeding up, driven by an unknown force named dark energy; dark energy makes up approximately 68.3-70% of the universe; it was recognized in the late 1990s from supernova observations; and Euclid will map billions of galaxies found up to 10 billion light-years from Earth. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: What is Dark Matter?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (canonical URL https://science.nasa.gov/dark-matter/). Supports: dark matter as the invisible material that makes up most of the matter in the universe; ordinary matter about 5%, dark matter about 27%, dark energy about 68%; dark matter does not absorb, reflect, or emit light; Vera Rubin's 1970s observations that stars at the outer edges of spiral galaxies move too fast to be held by the visible matter; and gravitational lensing by galaxy clusters revealing and mapping dark matter. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Galaxies: Large Scale Structures
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Supports: galaxy groups and clusters as collections of galaxies bound together by gravity; clusters also containing hot gas and dark matter; superclusters as large collections of clusters, groups, and individual galaxies (Local Group on the outer edges of the Laniakea supercluster); galactic walls such as the Sloan Great Wall spanning about 1.4 billion light-years; and the cosmic web as the twisting, threadlike arrangement of galaxies, groups, clusters, superclusters, and walls. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: 26.5 The Expanding Universe, Astronomy 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (server-rendered HTML). Supports: the discovery that the universe is expanding; Slipher's early spectra of spiral nebulae; Lemaître's 1927 paper suggesting an expanding universe; Hubble's 1929 velocity-distance relation and the 1931 Hubble and Humason paper showing recession velocities directly proportional to distances (speeds up to 20,000 km/s); Hubble's law as v = H x d with the Hubble constant; the textbook's unit convention of kilometers per second per million light-years with H converging near 22; and the worked arithmetic that a galaxy 100 million light-years away recedes at 2,200 km/s. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: 28.3 The Distribution of Galaxies in Space, Astronomy 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (server-rendered HTML). Supports: the Local Group (spread over about 3 million light-years, about 60 members including the Milky Way, Andromeda, and M33); rich galaxy clusters with thousands or tens of thousands of galaxies (Virgo Cluster about 50 million light-years away); superclusters as filamentary structures extending hundreds of millions of light-years in two dimensions but only 10-20 million light-years thick (the Virgo Supercluster); voids with typical diameters of 150 million light-years; and the sponge- or honeycomb-like arrangement of filaments and voids. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: 28.4 The Challenge of Dark Matter, Astronomy 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (server-rendered HTML). Supports: rotation curves as plots of velocity versus distance from a galaxy's center showing that dark matter forms a large halo around the luminous parts of galaxies (halos around the Milky Way and Andromeda possibly as large as 300,000 light-years); the motions of galaxies within clusters indicating cluster dark matter; and gravitational lensing by clusters, where lensed arcs and streaks of background galaxies allow astronomers to map how much mass a cluster contains and how it is distributed. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: 29.5 What Is the Universe Really Made Of?, Astronomy 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (server-rendered HTML). Supports: the composition of the universe (about 5% ordinary matter, about 27% dark matter, about 68% dark energy by mass-energy equivalent; only about half of one percent of the critical density is in stars); dark matter and dark energy accounting for about 95% of the universe's contents and not yet detected in earthbound laboratories; and supernova measurements at roughly half the universe's current age indicating that the expansion rate has sped up since those explosions. Facts synthesized in original wording.
